rules.title: A separate partition is created for containers
rules.explanation: Docker stores container images, layers, and metadata under /var/lib/docker by default. On many Linux installations this path resides on the root (/) or /var filesystem rather than on a dedicated volume.
rules.impact: Growth of images, containers, and volumes can fill /var/lib/docker and exhaust space on the host filesystem that also hosts critical OS data. Isolating Docker storage on a separate partition or logical volume contains disk consumption and reduces the risk that Docker activity renders the host unusable.

rules.title: A separate partition is created for containers
rules.explanation: Docker stores container images, layers, and metadata under /var/lib/docker by default. On many Linux installations this path resides on the root (/) or /var filesystem rather than on a dedicated volume.
rules.impact: Growth of images, containers, and volumes can fill /var/lib/docker and exhaust space on the host filesystem that also hosts critical OS data. Isolating Docker storage on a separate partition or logical volume contains disk consumption and reduces the risk that Docker activity renders the host unusable.

rules.title: Only trusted users can control the Docker daemon
rules.explanation: The Docker daemon exposes its API through a Unix socket that is typically owned by root and the docker group. Membership in the docker group grants the ability to communicate with the daemon.
rules.impact: Anyone who can talk to the Docker daemon can start containers that mount host paths such as /, effectively gaining root-equivalent control of the host. Restricting docker group membership to trusted administrators limits this privilege-escalation path.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for the Docker daemon
rules.explanation: The Docker daemon is a privileged host service that creates and manages containers. Linux audit rules can record access to the daemon binary and related activity alongside ordinary filesystem and syscall auditing.
rules.impact: Audit records of Docker daemon use support detection of unauthorized container operations and forensic investigation after an incident. Without daemon auditing, privileged container-platform activity may leave little durable evidence on the host.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — /run/containerd
rules.explanation: /run/containerd holds runtime state used by the containerd shim and related container lifecycle components that Docker relies on. The Docker and containerd services typically run with elevated privileges and depend on this directory.
rules.impact: Auditing /run/containerd helps detect unauthorized changes to container runtime state. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — /var/lib/docker
rules.explanation: /var/lib/docker is the default Docker data root and contains images, container writable layers, volumes, and related metadata. The Docker daemon runs with elevated privileges and depends on this directory.
rules.impact: Auditing /var/lib/docker helps detect unauthorized modification or access to container images and data. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — /etc/docker
rules.explanation: /etc/docker holds Docker daemon configuration and often TLS certificates and keys used for authenticated communication between clients and the daemon. The Docker daemon runs with elevated privileges and depends on this directory.
rules.impact: Auditing /etc/docker helps detect unauthorized changes to daemon configuration or credential material. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — docker.service
rules.explanation: The docker.service unit file defines how systemd starts the Docker daemon and may include administrator-supplied daemon options. When present, it influences privileged daemon behavior on the host.
rules.impact: Auditing docker.service helps detect unauthorized changes to Docker startup parameters. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — containerd.sock
rules.explanation: containerd.sock is the API socket used to communicate with the containerd runtime that Docker uses to create and manage containers. Access to this socket confers powerful control over container lifecycle operations.
rules.impact: Auditing containerd.sock helps detect unauthorized interaction with the container runtime. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — docker.sock
rules.explanation: docker.sock is the default Unix socket for the Docker Engine API. Clients that can read and write this socket can issue Docker commands with the privileges of the daemon.
rules.impact: Auditing docker.sock helps detect unauthorized use of the Docker API. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — /etc/default/docker
rules.explanation: /etc/default/docker is an environment file used on some distributions to supply Docker daemon options at service start. When present, it can alter privileged daemon behavior.
rules.impact: Auditing /etc/default/docker helps detect unauthorized changes to daemon startup options. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — /etc/docker/daemon.json
rules.explanation: /etc/docker/daemon.json is the Docker daemon configuration file and can define networking, logging, storage, TLS, and other runtime options. When present, it directly shapes daemon behavior.
rules.impact: Auditing /etc/docker/daemon.json helps detect unauthorized changes to daemon configuration. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — /etc/containerd/config.toml
rules.explanation: /etc/containerd/config.toml is the containerd configuration file and can define runtime, gRPC, and related settings used when Docker manages containers through containerd. When present, it influences container runtime behavior.
rules.impact: Auditing /etc/containerd/config.toml helps detect unauthorized changes to the container runtime configuration. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — /etc/sysconfig/docker
rules.explanation: /etc/sysconfig/docker is an environment or options file used on CentOS- and RHEL-based distributions to supply Docker daemon parameters at service start. When present, it can alter privileged daemon behavior.
rules.impact: Auditing /etc/sysconfig/docker helps detect unauthorized changes to daemon startup options. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — /usr/bin/containerd
rules.explanation: /usr/bin/containerd is the containerd runtime binary used by Docker to create and manage containers. It typically runs with elevated privileges on the host.
rules.impact: Auditing /usr/bin/containerd helps detect replacement or unexpected execution of the container runtime. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — /usr/bin/containerd-shim
rules.explanation: /usr/bin/containerd-shim is a containerd shim binary involved in supervising container processes. It is part of the privileged container runtime path used by Docker.
rules.impact: Auditing /usr/bin/containerd-shim helps detect tampering with container process supervision components. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — /usr/bin/containerd-shim-runc-v1
rules.explanation: /usr/bin/containerd-shim-runc-v1 is a containerd shim binary used with the runc runtime to supervise container processes. It is part of the privileged container runtime path used by Docker.
rules.impact: Auditing /usr/bin/containerd-shim-runc-v1 helps detect tampering with container process supervision components. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — /usr/bin/containerd-shim-runc-v2
rules.explanation: /usr/bin/containerd-shim-runc-v2 is a containerd shim binary used with the runc runtime to supervise container processes. It is part of the privileged container runtime path used by Docker.
rules.impact: Auditing /usr/bin/containerd-shim-runc-v2 helps detect tampering with container process supervision components. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: Auditing is configured for Docker files and directories — /usr/bin/runc
rules.explanation: /usr/bin/runc is the low-level OCI runtime that creates and runs containers on behalf of containerd and Docker. It typically executes with elevated privileges on the host.
rules.impact: Auditing /usr/bin/runc helps detect replacement or unexpected use of the container runtime binary. Audit logging can generate substantial volume, so log rotation and adequate storage for audit data remain important operational considerations.

rules.title: The Docker version is up to date
rules.explanation: Docker Engine releases include security fixes, bug fixes, and feature updates. Organizations typically track supported versions and apply updates according to their change-management and security policies.
rules.impact: Running an outdated Docker Engine leaves known vulnerabilities available for exploitation, which can lead to unauthorized access or privilege escalation on the host. Keeping Docker current within the versions required by applications reduces exposure to publicly documented defects.

rules.title: The Docker daemon runs as a non-root user where possible
rules.explanation: In rootless mode, the Docker daemon and containers run inside a user namespace so that neither the daemon nor container processes require host root privileges.
rules.impact: Rootless operation limits the blast radius of daemon or runtime vulnerabilities by keeping Docker components mapped to an unprivileged host user. Where workloads permit rootless mode, this reduces the likelihood that a container-platform compromise yields full host control.

rules.title: Network traffic between containers on the default bridge is restricted
rules.explanation: On the default Docker bridge network, containers on the same host can typically communicate freely with one another. Administrators can disable inter-container communication on that bridge, link specific containers, or place only required containers on user-defined networks.
rules.impact: Unrestricted bridge traffic allows each container to observe or reach peers on the same host network, which can lead to unintended information disclosure or lateral movement. Restricting default-bridge communication limits that exposure to explicitly intended paths.

rules.title: The logging level is set to info
rules.explanation: The Docker daemon log level controls how much detail is written to daemon logs. The info level records operational events while excluding verbose debug output.
rules.impact: An appropriate log level retains events needed for operations and incident review without flooding logs with debug noise. Running the daemon at debug level is generally reserved for troubleshooting because it increases volume and may expose additional internal detail.

rules.title: Docker is allowed to make changes to iptables
rules.explanation: iptables maintains IP packet filtering rules in the Linux kernel. The Docker daemon can automatically insert and update rules so that published container ports and bridge networking function correctly.
rules.impact: When Docker cannot manage iptables, container networking often depends on manually maintained rules that are easy to misconfigure. Allowing the daemon to update iptables keeps container connectivity consistent and reduces the chance of accidental isolation or unintended exposure.

rules.title: Insecure registries are not used
rules.explanation: Docker treats a registry as secure when TLS is used and the host trusts the registry CA, typically via certificates under /etc/docker/certs.d/<registry-name>/. An insecure registry lacks valid TLS protection or a trusted certificate.
rules.impact: Insecure registries expose image pull and push traffic to interception and tampering. Once a registry is marked insecure, docker pull, docker push, and docker search may succeed without TLS errors, allowing continued use of an unprotected registry without clear warning.

rules.title: The aufs storage driver is not used
rules.explanation: aufs is a legacy Docker storage driver built on out-of-tree Linux kernel patches. Modern Docker Engine releases deprecate aufs in favor of maintained drivers such as overlay2.
rules.impact: aufs has a history of kernel stability issues and is unsupported on many distributions with current kernels. Continuing to use aufs increases operational risk and leaves the host on a storage path that is no longer a recommended Docker baseline.
rules.scope: Settings in Storage Driver for docker

rules.title: TLS authentication for the Docker daemon is configured
rules.explanation: The Docker daemon can be exposed over TCP in addition to its default local Unix socket. When remote API access is required, TLS client and server authentication can restrict which hosts may connect.
rules.impact: Binding the daemon to a TCP port without TLS allows anyone who can reach that port to control Docker with daemon privileges, which is effectively host root access. TLS authentication limits remote daemon access to clients that present trusted certificates.

rules.title: Authorization for Docker client commands is enabled
rules.explanation: Docker authorization plugins and some third-party integrations can enforce fine-grained policies on Docker API requests beyond the default access model. The daemon can be configured to consult such an authorization mechanism for client commands.
rules.impact: The default Docker authorization model is all-or-nothing: any principal that can reach the daemon may run any Docker command. Authorization plugins reduce that risk by enforcing least-privilege access policies for local and remote API users.

rules.title: Centralized and remote logging is configured
rules.explanation: Docker supports multiple logging drivers that can send container and daemon logs to local files or to remote and centralized collectors. Preferred designs keep logs available outside the individual container host.
rules.impact: Centralized remote logging preserves audit and diagnostic records if a host or container is compromised, rebuilt, or loses local storage. Aligning the Docker log driver with organizational logging standards improves incident response and monitoring coverage.

rules.title: Containers cannot gain new privileges
rules.explanation: The no-new-privileges setting prevents processes from gaining additional privileges through setuid or setgid binaries. Docker can enable this default for new containers via daemon configuration.
rules.impact: Blocking new privileges reduces the usefulness of setuid and setgid binaries as escalation paths inside containers. Applying the setting at the daemon level establishes a safer default for subsequently created containers.

rules.title: The userland proxy is disabled
rules.explanation: When ports are published, Docker can forward traffic using kernel NAT or a user-space proxy process (userland-proxy). Where hairpin NAT is available, the userland proxy is often unnecessary.
rules.impact: Disabling the userland proxy removes an extra network-facing component from the host attack surface and typically improves port-forwarding performance by relying on native iptables NAT. Where NAT meets requirements, the proxy adds little benefit relative to its exposure.

rules.title: A custom seccomp profile is applied daemon-wide when required
rules.explanation: seccomp filters the system calls a process may issue. Docker ships a default seccomp profile, and administrators can apply a custom profile daemon-wide when organizational policy requires a different syscall allow list.
rules.impact: Limiting available system calls reduces the kernel attack surface exposed to containerized workloads. A custom profile is useful when the default Docker profile does not match policy; otherwise the default profile already provides meaningful syscall restriction.

rules.title: Experimental features are not enabled in production
rules.explanation: Docker Engine can enable experimental features with a daemon runtime flag such as --experimental. Experimental capabilities are packaged with the daemon rather than delivered only as a separate build.
rules.impact: Experimental features may be less thoroughly validated and may change without the stability guarantees expected in production. Keeping experimental mode disabled on production hosts avoids unintended reliance on unfinished or mutable daemon behavior.

rules.title: Ownership of docker.service is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The docker.service unit file controls how systemd starts the Docker daemon and may contain sensitive ExecStart options. Ownership is typically expected to be root:root.
rules.impact: If a less-privileged user can change docker.service, that user can alter daemon startup parameters and potentially subvert Docker on the host. root:root ownership helps preserve integrity of this privileged unit file.

rules.title: Permissions on docker.service are set to 644 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: File mode bits on docker.service determine who may read or modify the systemd unit that starts the Docker daemon. Permissions of 644 or stricter limit write access appropriately.
rules.impact: Writable docker.service content would allow non-root users to change daemon launch options. Restrictive permissions help ensure only root can modify this sensitive unit file.

rules.title: Ownership of docker.socket is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The docker.socket unit file defines the systemd socket activation settings for the Docker API socket and can influence how the remote or local API is exposed. Ownership is typically expected to be root:root.
rules.impact: Unauthorized modification of docker.socket can change how the Docker API socket is created or exposed. root:root ownership helps prevent less-privileged users from altering this sensitive unit file.

rules.title: Permissions on docker.socket are set to 644 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: File mode bits on docker.socket determine who may read or modify the systemd socket unit associated with the Docker API. Permissions of 644 or stricter limit write access appropriately.
rules.impact: If docker.socket is writable by non-root users, API socket activation settings can be changed without authorization. Restrictive permissions help preserve control over Docker API exposure.

rules.title: Ownership of /etc/docker is set to root:root
rules.explanation: /etc/docker contains Docker daemon configuration and frequently stores TLS certificates and keys. Directory ownership is typically expected to be root:root.
rules.impact: Loose ownership of /etc/docker can allow less-privileged users to alter configuration or credential material used by the daemon. root:root ownership helps protect these sensitive files.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/docker are set to 755 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: Permissions on /etc/docker control who may traverse or modify the Docker configuration directory, which often includes certificates and keys. Mode 755 or stricter is the expected baseline.
rules.impact: Write access to /etc/docker for non-root users would allow unauthorized changes to daemon configuration or credentials. Restrictive permissions help keep that directory under administrative control.

rules.title: Ownership of registry certificate files is set to root:root
rules.explanation: Registry CA and client certificate files used by Docker are commonly stored under /etc/docker/certs.d/<registry-name>/. These files should be owned by root:root when present.
rules.impact: If registry certificate files can be replaced by a less-privileged user, Docker may be directed to trust a malicious registry or fail open to tampering. root:root ownership helps protect registry trust anchors.

rules.title: Permissions on registry certificate files are set to 444 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: Registry certificate files under /etc/docker/certs.d/<registry-name>/ establish trust for private registries. When those files exist, permissions of 444 or stricter limit modification.
rules.impact: Overly permissive certificate files increase the chance of unauthorized alteration of registry trust material. Restrictive modes help preserve the integrity of certificates Docker uses for registry TLS.

rules.title: Ownership of the TLS CA certificate file is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The TLS CA certificate supplied to the daemon (for example via --tlscacert) is used to validate Docker client certificates. It should be owned by root:root.
rules.impact: Replacement of the TLS CA certificate could allow unauthorized clients to authenticate to the Docker daemon. root:root ownership helps protect this trust anchor from tampering.

rules.title: Permissions on the TLS CA certificate file are set to 444 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: The TLS CA certificate file passed with --tlscacert authenticates Docker clients against a given CA. Permissions of 444 or stricter limit who can modify that file.
rules.impact: Writable CA material weakens TLS authentication for the Docker API. Restrictive permissions help ensure less-privileged users cannot alter the CA certificate the daemon trusts.

rules.title: Ownership of the Docker server certificate file is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The Docker daemon server certificate (for example via --tlscert) identifies the daemon to TLS clients. It should be owned by root:root.
rules.impact: Unauthorized replacement of the server certificate can enable impersonation of the Docker API endpoint. root:root ownership helps protect the certificate used for daemon TLS identity.

rules.title: Permissions on the Docker server certificate file are set to 444 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: The Docker server certificate file passed with --tlscert presents the daemon identity during TLS handshakes. Permissions of 444 or stricter limit modification of that file.
rules.impact: If the server certificate can be modified by less-privileged users, clients may be misled about daemon identity. Restrictive permissions help preserve TLS server authenticity.

rules.title: Ownership of the Docker server certificate key file is set to root:root
rules.explanation: The Docker server private key (for example via --tlskey) pairs with the daemon TLS certificate. It should be owned by root:root.
rules.impact: Disclosure or replacement of the server private key allows impersonation of the Docker daemon over TLS. root:root ownership helps keep this credential under administrative control.

rules.title: Permissions on the Docker server certificate key file are set to 400
rules.explanation: The Docker server certificate key file passed with --tlskey holds the private key for daemon TLS. Mode 400 restricts access to the owning user, typically root.
rules.impact: A readable or writable private key can be copied or altered by unauthorized parties, defeating Docker daemon TLS. Permissions of 400 help confine key access to the owner.

rules.title: Ownership of the Docker socket file is set to root:docker
rules.explanation: The default Docker Unix socket (commonly /var/run/docker.sock) is the local Engine API endpoint. It is expected to be owned by user root and group docker.
rules.impact: Socket ownership outside root:docker can let unintended users or groups issue Docker API calls with daemon privileges. Keeping ownership at root:docker preserves the intended administrative trust boundary for local Docker access.

rules.title: Permissions on the Docker socket file are set to 660 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: Permissions on the Docker Unix socket determine which users may speak to the Docker Engine API locally. Mode 660 or stricter limits access to the owner and group.
rules.impact: Broader socket permissions allow users outside the docker group to control the daemon. Restrictive modes help ensure only root and approved docker group members can use the API.

rules.title: Ownership of daemon.json is set to root:root
rules.explanation: When present, /etc/docker/daemon.json supplies Docker daemon configuration such as networking, logging, and security options. Ownership is typically expected to be root:root.
rules.impact: Unauthorized changes to daemon.json can weaken host and container security controls enforced by the daemon. root:root ownership helps prevent less-privileged users from altering those settings.

rules.title: Permissions on daemon.json are set to 644 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: File permissions on daemon.json control who may modify Docker daemon configuration when the file is present. Mode 644 or stricter is the expected baseline.
rules.impact: Writable daemon.json content for non-root users would allow unauthorized reconfiguration of the Docker Engine. Restrictive permissions help keep daemon settings under administrative control.

rules.title: Ownership of /etc/default/docker is set to root:root
rules.explanation: /etc/default/docker can provide environment-based options for the Docker daemon on some distributions. When the file exists, ownership is typically expected to be root:root.
rules.impact: If less-privileged users can edit /etc/default/docker, they may change daemon startup behavior. root:root ownership helps protect those sensitive parameters.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/default/docker are set to 644 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: Permissions on /etc/default/docker determine who may modify Docker daemon options supplied through that environment file. Mode 644 or stricter is the expected baseline when the file exists.
rules.impact: Overly permissive modes allow unauthorized alteration of daemon startup settings. Restrictive permissions help ensure only root can change /etc/default/docker.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/sysconfig/docker are set to 644 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: /etc/sysconfig/docker can supply Docker daemon options on CentOS- and RHEL-based systems. When present, permissions of 644 or stricter limit modification of that file.
rules.impact: Writable /etc/sysconfig/docker content for non-root users can change privileged daemon behavior. Restrictive permissions help keep those settings under administrative control.

rules.title: Ownership of /etc/sysconfig/docker is set to root:root
rules.explanation: /etc/sysconfig/docker holds sensitive parameters that can alter Docker daemon behavior on CentOS- and RHEL-based distributions. When present, ownership is typically expected to be root:root.
rules.impact: Unauthorized ownership changes could allow less-privileged users to modify daemon startup options. root:root ownership helps preserve integrity of this configuration file.

rules.title: Ownership of the containerd socket file is set to root:root
rules.explanation: containerd exposes an API Unix socket (commonly /run/containerd/containerd.sock) used to manage containers. Unlike docker.sock, ordinary users typically do not require access, so ownership is expected to be root:root.
rules.impact: If an unprivileged user or unexpected group owns the containerd socket, that principal can interact with the container runtime and containers. root:root ownership reduces unauthorized runtime control.

rules.title: Permissions on the containerd socket file are set to 660 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: Permissions on the containerd Unix socket determine who may call the containerd API. Mode 660 or stricter limits read and write access to the owner and group, typically root.
rules.impact: Broader permissions on containerd.sock expand who can create, start, or otherwise control containers through containerd. Restrictive modes help confine runtime API access to administrators.

rules.title: Containers are configured to run as a non-root user
rules.explanation: Container processes inherit the user defined by the image USER instruction or by runtime user settings. Containers can be built and run so that the primary process is a non-root user.
rules.impact: Running as root inside a container increases the impact of application compromise, especially when combined with additional host capabilities or mounts. A non-root container user reduces privilege available to an attacker after breakout of the application process.
rules.scope: Parameter for the Docker container user

rules.title: Docker Content Trust is enabled
rules.explanation: Docker Content Trust uses digital signatures so that clients can verify the publisher and integrity of image tags pulled from remote registries. The feature is controlled through environment settings such as DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST and is disabled by default.
rules.impact: Without content trust, clients may run images whose tags have been substituted or tampered with in transit or at the registry. Enabling signature verification strengthens assurance of image provenance before deployment.

rules.title: An AppArmor profile is enabled where applicable
rules.explanation: AppArmor is a Linux Mandatory Access Control framework available by default on distributions such as Debian and Ubuntu. Docker can apply the default AppArmor profile or a custom profile to containers.
rules.impact: An AppArmor profile constrains the operations a containerized process may perform on the host, reducing the impact of application compromise. Enabling AppArmor where the host supports it adds a policy enforcement layer around containers.

rules.title: SELinux security options are configured where applicable
rules.explanation: SELinux is a Linux Mandatory Access Control framework commonly enabled on distributions such as Red Hat Enterprise Linux and Fedora. Docker can label containers so that SELinux policy applies to their processes and file access.
rules.impact: Correct SELinux labeling confines container processes according to host policy and limits damage from breakout attempts. Misconfigured policy can disrupt workloads, but omitting SELinux where it is available forgoes an important isolation control.

rules.title: Linux kernel capabilities within containers are restricted
rules.explanation: Docker starts containers with a reduced set of Linux capabilities rather than full root capability sets. Capabilities such as NET_RAW can still be present in the default set and may be dropped when not required.
rules.impact: Unnecessary capabilities expand what a compromised container process can do on the network or host interfaces. Dropping unneeded capabilities, including NET_RAW unless explicitly required, shrinks the container attack surface.

rules.title: Privileged containers are not used
rules.explanation: The --privileged flag grants a container nearly all Linux capabilities and relaxes device cgroup restrictions, overriding finer --cap-add and --cap-drop settings. Privileged mode is intended only for specialized use cases.
rules.impact: A privileged container has broad access comparable to processes on the host and can manipulate devices and kernel features that ordinary containers cannot. Avoiding privileged mode preserves capability and device isolation for typical workloads.

rules.title: Sensitive host system directories are not mounted into containers
rules.explanation: Docker volumes and bind mounts can map host directories into a container filesystem, including sensitive paths, in read-only or read-write mode.
rules.impact: Read-write mounts of sensitive host directories allow container processes to alter critical host files and configurations. Avoiding such mounts, especially writable ones, reduces host compromise risk from container workloads.

rules.title: Sshd is not run inside containers
rules.explanation: An SSH daemon can be installed and started inside a container image, exposing remote shell access to that container. Administrative access is alternatively available from the Docker host using tools such as docker exec.
rules.impact: Running sshd in containers multiplies key, password, patching, and access-policy management burdens across images. Eliminating in-container SSH reduces unnecessary network services and keeps remote administration on the hardened host path.

rules.title: Privileged ports are not mapped within containers
rules.explanation: TCP and UDP ports below 1024 are privileged host ports. Docker can publish a container port to a privileged host port when the mapping is declared explicitly, even though automatic allocation normally uses high ephemeral ports.
rules.impact: Privileged ports often carry security-sensitive services and traffic. Allowing containers to bind them expands exposure of those ports to containerized workloads and conflicts with least-privilege network practice on the host.

rules.title: The container root filesystem is mounted read-only
rules.explanation: The Docker --read-only runtime option mounts the container root filesystem as read-only so that the running instance cannot write to the image layers. Writable state then depends on explicit volumes or temporary filesystems.
rules.impact: A read-only root filesystem enforces immutable infrastructure at runtime and prevents many forms of in-container persistence or binary replacement. Attackers have fewer places to plant malware when writes require deliberately mounted paths.

rules.title: Incoming container traffic is bound to a specific host interface
rules.explanation: Published container ports can listen on all host addresses or on a specific host IP associated with one network interface. Binding to a chosen interface limits where inbound traffic is accepted.
rules.impact: Listening on 0.0.0.0 or equivalent exposes published services on every host interface, including networks not intended for that workload. Binding to a specific interface keeps inbound access on the path where inspection and filtering controls are applied.

rules.title: The host PID namespace is not shared
rules.explanation: PID namespaces isolate process ID spaces so that containers cannot see host processes by default. Sharing the host PID namespace makes host processes visible inside the container.
rules.impact: With the host PID namespace shared, a container can observe, signal, or interfere with processes on the host, weakening process isolation. In multi-tenant environments this can enable denial of service or aid further compromise of the host.
rules.scope: PID parameters for processes in Docker containers

rules.title: The host IPC namespace is not shared
rules.explanation: IPC namespaces isolate System V and POSIX IPC objects such as shared memory segments, semaphores, and message queues. Containers receive a private IPC namespace unless the host IPC namespace is shared.
rules.impact: Sharing host IPC lets container processes interact with host IPC objects and removes IPC isolation between tenants and the host. That exposure can leak data or enable interference with host processes that rely on IPC.

rules.title: Host devices are not directly exposed to containers
rules.explanation: The --device option maps host device nodes into a container so the workload can access hardware or block devices without full privileged mode.
rules.impact: Direct device exposure can allow containers to read, write, or manage sensitive host devices, including removing block devices in some cases. Keeping devices off untrusted containers preserves device isolation on the host.

rules.title: The mount propagation mode is not set to shared
rules.explanation: Mount propagation controls whether mount and unmount events on a volume are visible to other mount points. Docker volumes can use private or shared propagation modes.
rules.impact: Shared propagation replicates mounts across related mount points and can allow other containers to observe or influence those mounts. Unless shared mode is explicitly required, avoiding it limits unexpected cross-container filesystem coupling.

rules.title: The host UTS namespace is not shared
rules.explanation: UTS namespaces isolate hostname and NIS domain name. Containers normally receive their own UTS namespace so they do not share the host identity identifiers.
rules.impact: Sharing the host UTS namespace can allow a container to change the host hostname or domain name. That capability is unnecessary for most workloads and weakens host identity isolation.

rules.title: The default seccomp profile is not disabled
rules.explanation: Docker applies a default seccomp profile that allow-lists commonly needed system calls and blocks others. The profile can be disabled for a container when an application is incompatible with the filter.
rules.impact: Disabling seccomp restores a much larger syscall surface to the container process and increases the chance that kernel vulnerabilities can be reached. Keeping the default profile enabled preserves an important runtime hardening control.

rules.title: Docker exec is not used with the --privileged option
rules.explanation: docker exec can start a process in a running container with the --privileged option, which grants additional Linux capabilities to that exec session.
rules.impact: A privileged exec session can bypass capability restrictions that were applied when the container started. Avoiding --privileged with docker exec helps preserve the container's intended least-privilege posture during operational access.

rules.title: Docker exec is not used with the --user=root option
rules.explanation: docker exec accepts a --user option that selects the user for the executed process inside the container. Specifying root runs that session as UID 0 in the container user namespace.
rules.impact: Executing as root via docker exec can override a non-root container design and grant elevated rights inside the workload for troubleshooting commands. Avoiding --user=root helps keep interactive access aligned with the container's least-privilege user.

rules.title: Cgroup usage is confirmed
rules.explanation: Containers run under Linux control groups (cgroups) that limit and account for resources. Docker places containers in a default cgroup hierarchy unless a different cgroup parent is specified.
rules.impact: Attaching a container to an unexpected cgroup parent can grant different resource limits or hierarchical permissions than operators intended. Confirming cgroup placement helps prevent accidental privilege or resource-boundary bypass.

rules.title: The container is restricted from gaining additional privileges
rules.explanation: The no-new-privileges security option prevents a container process from acquiring additional privileges through setuid or setgid binaries after it starts.
rules.impact: Without this restriction, a compromised process may escalate by executing setuid helpers inside the image. Enforcing no-new-privileges reduces that escalation path for container workloads.

rules.title: The default docker0 bridge is not used
rules.explanation: docker0 is the default Docker Linux bridge to which containers attach in the traditional bridge networking model. User-defined networks provide alternative connectivity with more explicit composition.
rules.impact: The default bridge model has historically been more exposed to ARP spoofing and MAC flooding concerns because filtering is limited. Preferring user-defined networks reduces reliance on that shared default bridge for application traffic.

rules.title: The host user namespace is not shared
rules.explanation: User namespaces map container UIDs and GIDs to different host identities so that container root need not equal host root. Sharing the host user namespace disables that remapping for the container.
rules.impact: When the host user namespace is shared, container user identities align with host users and the isolation benefit of user namespaces is lost. Keeping user namespaces unshared preserves an important boundary between container and host privileges.

rules.title: The Docker socket is not mounted inside containers
rules.explanation: The Docker API socket docker.sock can be bind-mounted into a container filesystem, giving processes inside that container direct access to the Engine API.
rules.impact: A mounted Docker socket effectively grants container processes control of the Docker daemon and thereby of the host. Keeping docker.sock out of containers prevents this common container-escape and host-takeover pattern.

rules.title: Swarm services are bound to a specific host interface
rules.explanation: Docker Swarm manager control traffic listens on an address configured with --listen-addr, which defaults to 0.0.0.0:2377 and therefore all host interfaces. A specific IP can limit listeners to one interface.
rules.impact: Listening on all interfaces can expose Swarm management ports to networks that are not part of the cluster trust boundary. Binding to a dedicated interface reduces unintended remote access to Swarm control plane services.

rules.title: Docker Swarm overlay networks are encrypted
rules.explanation: Swarm overlay networks connect containers across nodes. Encryption can be enabled with overlay network options so that node-to-node application traffic on the overlay is protected.
rules.impact: Unencrypted overlay traffic may be observable on the underlay network between Swarm nodes, disclosing application data in transit. Enabling overlay encryption protects confidentiality of cross-node container communications.
rules.scope: --opt encrypted parameter for the Docker Swarm network

rules.title: Docker secret management commands are used for Swarm secrets
rules.explanation: Docker Swarm includes built-in secret objects and CLI commands for creating and distributing secrets to services. Secrets are designed for sensitive values such as passwords, tokens, and keys within the cluster.
rules.impact: Managing sensitive material through Swarm secrets avoids baking credentials into images or environment variables that are easier to extract. Using the native secret workflow improves control and auditability of secret distribution in the swarm.

rules.title: The Swarm manager runs with autolock enabled
rules.explanation: Swarm autolock requires a manager unlock key after Docker restarts before cluster encryption keys are loaded into memory. The feature is enabled with --autolock when initializing or updating the swarm.
rules.impact: Autolock protects the TLS key material used between swarm nodes and the keys that encrypt Raft logs at rest when a manager host reboots. This strengthens key protection in high-security environments, at the cost of requiring an unlock step before managers resume automatically.

rules.title: The Swarm manager autolock key is rotated periodically
rules.explanation: The Swarm manager autolock unlock key is a static secret until an administrator rotates it. Docker provides commands to rotate that key as part of ongoing key lifecycle management.
rules.impact: An unrotated unlock key that is disclosed remains valid indefinitely and can unlock managers after restart. Periodic rotation limits the useful lifetime of a compromised autolock key.

rules.title: Swarm node certificates are rotated appropriately
rules.explanation: Docker Swarm issues TLS certificates to nodes for cluster membership and mutual authentication. Certificate lifetime is configurable (for example via --cert-expiry) and certificates renew on a schedule such as the default 90-day period.
rules.impact: Regular node certificate rotation limits how long a stolen node credential remains valid for impersonation within the swarm. Aligning rotation frequency with organizational policy reduces lingering trust in compromised nodes or keys.
rules.scope: The --cert-expiry parameter for Docker Swarm certificates

rules.title: Swarm CA certificates are rotated properly
rules.explanation: Docker Swarm relies on a cluster root CA to issue node certificates for TLS between managers and workers. Root CA rotation is an administrative operation and is not performed automatically by default.
rules.impact: Node certificates inherit trust from the swarm CA, so a compromised CA key undermines node identity across the cluster. Periodic CA rotation according to policy reduces long-term exposure of that root of trust.
rules.scope: ca --rotate parameter for Docker Swarm secret

rules.title: Management plane traffic is separated from data traffic
rules.explanation: Swarm and Docker hosts can advertise and carry cluster management traffic on addresses distinct from application data paths, for example via --advertise-addr and --data-path-addr during swarm initialization.
rules.impact: Separating management and data planes isolates control traffic for monitoring and policy enforcement and helps keep cluster administration reachable during data-plane congestion or attack. Mixed planes increase the chance that application traffic floods or exposures affect management availability.
rules.scope: The swarm init --advertise-addr= --data-path-addr= parameter when initializing Docker Swarm

rules.title: The container host is hardened
rules.explanation: The container host is the Linux (or other) operating system that runs the Docker Engine and one or more containers. Host configuration, patching, and access controls sit outside the container runtime itself.
rules.impact: Weak host hardening undermines container isolation because containers share the host kernel and many host resources. A compromised or poorly configured host can expose every container workload running on it.
rules.scope: Parameters are not specified; follow general host hardening recommendations.

rules.title: Default ulimit values are configured appropriately
rules.explanation: ulimit settings constrain resources such as open files and processes available to a program. Docker can set default ulimits for containers through daemon options such as --default-ulimit or daemon.json.
rules.impact: Absent or overly permissive ulimits allow a single container process to exhaust host resources and disrupt other workloads. Sensible defaults reduce denial-of-service risk from runaway or malicious processes.

rules.title: User namespace remapping is enabled
rules.explanation: User namespace remapping maps container UIDs and GIDs onto subordinate ranges on the host, typically configured with userns-remap and files such as /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid. Container root then corresponds to an unprivileged host identity.
rules.impact: Without user namespace remapping, container UID 0 aligns with host root for many filesystem operations when volumes are involved. Remapping adds a privilege boundary that limits the impact of container breakout on the host user identity space.

rules.title: Default cgroup usage is confirmed
rules.explanation: Docker places containers under a default cgroup parent unless --cgroup-parent or equivalent configuration specifies another hierarchy. Operators can verify that containers remain in the intended default unless a deliberate change is required.
rules.impact: Unexpected cgroup parents can alter resource accounting and hierarchical limits applied to containers. Confirming default cgroup usage helps ensure workloads do not inherit unintended privileges or resource boundaries.
rules.scope: Parameter: --cgroup-parent (must be empty or meet requirements).

rules.title: The device base size is not changed unless necessary
rules.explanation: For certain storage drivers, dm.basesize (via storage-opt) sets the thin-pool base device size available to containers. Leaving the default avoids enlarging per-container storage beyond what the environment requires.
rules.impact: Increasing dm.basesize can accelerate host storage consumption as containers allocate larger writable layers. Changing the base size only when necessary helps prevent resource exhaustion on the Docker host.
rules.scope: Parameter: --storage-opt dm.basesize (must not be used unless necessary).

rules.title: Setuid and setgid bits are removed where not required
rules.explanation: setuid and setgid permission bits allow executables to run with the file owner's or group's privileges. Container images may contain such binaries even when the application does not need them.
rules.impact: Unnecessary setuid or setgid binaries inside images provide ready privilege-escalation helpers after application compromise. Removing those bits where they are not required reduces escalation options within the container.

rules.title: Only trusted packages are installed in images
rules.explanation: Container images are often built by installing OS or language packages from remote repositories. Package authenticity can be verified using mechanisms such as GPG-signed repositories before software is added to an image.
rules.impact: Unverified packages may introduce vulnerable or malicious components into production images. Installing only trusted, authenticity-checked packages reduces supply-chain risk in container builds.
rules.scope: Use of GPG keys or other verification mechanisms.

rules.title: Signed artifacts are verified before use
rules.explanation: Build and deployment pipelines can consume signed container-related artifacts such as images or packages. Signature verification confirms that artifacts match an expected publisher and have not been altered.
rules.impact: Using artifacts without verifying signatures weakens assurance of integrity and provenance. Verification helps prevent deployment of tampered or substituted components into the Docker environment.

rules.title: Only necessary ports are published on containers
rules.explanation: Docker publishes container ports to the host with options such as -p/--publish, which can expose services on host interfaces. Only ports required for the workload need to be published.
rules.impact: Each published port expands the network attack surface reachable from host or external networks. Limiting publications to necessary ports reduces opportunities for unauthorized access to container services.
